The Banggai cardinalfish Pterapogon kauderni exhibits a suite of life-history traits shaped by its endemic reef habitat. At birth, newly emerged juveniles, which are mouthbrooded by the male, possess a remarkably small wet weight of just 0.014 grams [Wwb = 0.014 grams]. This minimal initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves of the egg, which has an approximate diameter of three millimeters. These tiny recruits are immediately independent upon release from the paternal buccal cavity. Field observations indicate that females ultimately achieve a substantially larger body size, with an ultimate wet weight of 10.2 grams [Wwi = 10.2 grams] recorded in gravid individuals. This more than seven-hundred-fold increase in mass from birth to adulthood underscores a rapid growth phase during the juvenile and sub-adult stages, a pattern common among small-bodied, site-attached coral reef fishes. The ultimate standard length of the species has been measured at 8.6 centimeters [Li = 8.6 centimeters], a modest size that confines adults to microhabitats within shallow seagrass beds and among the spines of sea urchins.

Sexual maturation in this cardinalfish is tied to the attainment of a moderate body length rather than a strict chronological age. Individuals are considered to have reached the pubertal threshold upon achieving a standard length of 4.1 centimeters [Lp = 4.1 centimeters]. This length-at-puberty is a key demographic parameter, as it defines the onset of reproductive competence. In captive populations maintained at a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the transition from juvenile to reproductively active adult occurs after a period of several months. At this size, males develop the enlarged buccal cavity necessary for mouthbrooding, while females begin vitellogenesis. Compared to the ultimate length of 8.6 cm [Li = 8.6 cm], puberty occurs at roughly half the maximum attainable size, a typical pattern for iteroparous fish species that continue somatic growth after maturity. This energetic commitment to further growth even after the onset of reproductive activity is a central feature of their life-history strategy.

Reproductive effort in the Banggai cardinalfish is characterized by a high frequency of spawning events under favorable thermal conditions. At a constant water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a reproductively active female can produce a clutch of approximately 70 eggs per brood [N_R_i = approximately 70 eggs per brood]. The inter-brood interval is relatively short, with field observations reporting that females initiate a new clutch nearly every two to three weeks, yielding an annual event frequency of about 1 brood per year [F_R_i = about 1 brood per year]. This remarkably high reproductive rate is facilitated by the male's mouthbrooding behavior, which liberates the female from post-fertilization parental duties, allowing her to allocate energy directly to the next batch of oocytes. The thermal dependency of this reproductive output is evident, with the maximum rates being sustained only within a narrow thermal window; the reported values of 70 eggs per brood [N_R_i = 70 eggs per brood] and about 1 brood annually [F_R_i = about 1 brood annually] were documented under controlled laboratory conditions at 27 °C [T = 27 °C].

Longevity records for Pterapogon kauderni indicate a relatively extended lifespan for a fish of its diminutive size. In natural populations, the oldest individuals have been documented to survive for up to 6 years [am = up to 6 years] at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This lifespan, exceeding half a decade, is notably long compared to many other small-bodied, reef-associated teleosts, which often complete their life cycle in two to three years. The extended longevity is likely linked to the species' parental care strategy, which reduces early-life mortality, coupled with a relatively low adult predation rate within its sheltered microhabitat. In captivity, where environmental conditions and food availability are optimized at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], individuals can also routinely attain this maximum age of 6 years [am = 6 years], suggesting a strong genetic ceiling on lifespan. This extended period of senescence, combined with a high annual reproductive output, positions the species closer to a slow-fast continuum than its small body size might initially suggest.

A comparison of the species' asymptotic body mass provides a clear illustration of the substantial sexual dimorphism that exists in body size, despite both sexes reaching a similar ultimate length. While the ultimate wet weight for females reaches 10.2 grams [Wwi = 10.2 grams], the typical asymptotic mass for males is considerably lower, reflecting the fact that males do not carry the energetic burden of egg production. The difference in body mass between the sexes is further highlighted when considering the initial size at independence; a juvenile weighing only 0.014 grams [Wwb = 0.014 grams] at birth must undergo a massive growth trajectory to reach the female asymptotic mass of 10.2 grams [Wwi = 10.2 grams]. This growth is accomplished over the course of the species' maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years], a duration that allows for repeated spawning events at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. The growth pattern, from a minute newly released juvenile to a comparatively large adult female, is a continuous process that slows considerably after the onset of puberty at 4.1 centimeters [Lp = 4.1 centimeters] standard length.
